

SPEEDY USER DOCUMENTATION
---------------------------------

OVERVIEW
------------

"speedy" 

    A utility for doing interesting things with gate level chip
	designs.  Historicly attached to design files created using
	SUE.  Also, historicly the name "speedy" attaches to a method
	& implementation for automaticly adjusting cell sizes, but
	actually Speedy contains a "flat" representation of the chip
	layout (including logical and physical information);
	information that can be used to do all sorts of useful work at
	that level of design, sometimes known as "The Flat World" (as 
	opposed to the Hierarchical World of SUE).  Capabilities in
	place: 

		* timing analysis

		* cell size analysis

		* ideal routing (steiner routes) in support of DPC and
		  timing 

		* global routing (based on steiner net routes)
		  & congestion analysis  


    How does this work into a design flow?  Good question.

    Implementation:
	Speedy is implemented in C++ using an object-oriented
	methodology. Every effort has been made to avoid using the
	sneakier C++ tricks; there is no operator overloading,
	exceptions, nor even templates; and class hierarchies are used
	very sparingly.  "void *" pointers are never used. Every
	effort has been made to implement a uniform style and to make
	the source code as readable as can be done.

	I have not tried to trade of readability for micro-efficiency;
	today's optimizing compilers will have no difficulty creating
	efficient executable code from the source structures I am using.

	I hope the result is easy-to-read (even by "C" people),
	maintainable code.



SUE MODE & STANDALONE MODE
-----------------------------

    Speedy can run either as a standalone program or linked in to SUE.
	Most of the following assumes Sue mode; see below for 
	STANDALONE MODE.

    SUE mode 

	Sue is set to "speedy mode" by setting DPC_TIMING(simulator) 
	to "speedy". This can be done from some .suerc file:

		set DPC_TIMING(simulator) speedy

	or when Sue is invoked:

		sue -set DPC_TIMING(simulator)=speedy ...


	Speedy is invoked transparently when the user calls "dpc_it".
	Speedy will calculate and return to Sue timing information in
	exactly the style of Pearl, and also initialize itself so the
	all Speedy commands (see below) are available.

	Speedy commands are invoked from the Sue command line, prefixed
	with "speedy":

		sue> speedy <speedy command name> <speedy command arguments>

		NOTE: Since the Sue command line is Tcl-ish, brackets
		(as in "net_1[0]") are interpreted as part of the command
		syntax; to prevent this, such characters must be escaped 
		with a backslash: 
			sue> speedy print net net_1\[0\]



AUXILIARY FILES
---------------
    See FILE FORMATS, below

    control files:

	<design_name> is the name of the Sue cell that was dpc'd

	<design_name>.timing_in: generated by SUE during time_it, in
		particular proc setup_speedy, and somewhat
		unfortunately deleted when time_it is complete.
		Sets parameters for timing, such as assumed external
		output load capacitance	

	<design_name>.constraint: (".timing_in" format): generated 
		manually in the same format as the timing_in file, 
		used to override default values and make up new ones.

	<design_name>.timing_out: in SUE mode, written during time_it; 
		used to pass timing information back into SUE, where 
		it is displayed.

	speedy.cmd: in standalone mode, defines a set of commands
		to be executed on startup.  Other command files can
		be created and called explicitly or nested-ly.

	<design_name>.fixfile: place for random stuff.  Could just as 
		better go in constraint file, except that constraint 
		file format is defined to be PEARL, until we decide 
		otherwise.

    design source files:

	<various>.lib: timing information for cells; Speedy will load
		whatever is specified in DPC_TIMING(ctlf_file)

	<design_name>.vg: the verilog netlist that defines the design.
	
	


FILE FORMATS
-----------------------

   .timing_in/.constraint files:

	# <whatever>			comment
	<empty line>			no-op
	<other>				print warning message to console

	setmaxpossiblities <integer>	specify number of long paths
					  to be written to .timing_in

	toplevelcell <cell name>	set top level of DESIGN			

	readcapacitances <filename>	import .est_cap file
	readcelllibrary <filename>	import .lib file
	readdspf <filename>		import .dspf file
	readverilog <filename>		import .vg file

	inputslew <extconn name> <min_rise> <max_rise> <min_fall> <max_fall>
					set transition of external inputs 
					... speedy uses max_rise and max_fall, 
					  min_rise and min_fall are ignored

		<pin name> can be:
			*	all 	 
			<name>	
			<name>[<index>]
			<name>{<index>:<index] 

		<min_rise>, etc	must be (picoseconds):
			<integer>ps		

	setnodecapacitance <pin name> <capacitance>		
			set external load capacitance for external outputs

	
		<pin name> as for inputslew

		<capacitance> must be (femtofarads):
			<integer>fF


    .fixfile:

	# <whatever>			comment
	<empty line>			no-op
	<other>				print warning message to console

	dont_resize path <instance path>	
		disallow any resizeing of the instance with this pathname... 
		if a partial pathname is given, all leaf intances below 
		this node are marked

	dont_resize cell <cell type name>
		<cell type name> identifies a verilog module, whose
		name will apear as an element of the instance pathname.
		disallow any resizing of all instances within any 
		occurrance of this module

	is_flipflop_type <cell name>	force this cell to be treated
					as a flipflop for timing purposes

    

STATIC TIMING ANALYSIS
--------------------------

    Requires that "dpc_it" has previously been run. During "dpc_it", Speedy
	loads the DESIGN, does as much sanity checking as possible,  does
	a Steiner route, and quietly performs a global_timing.  The timing
	data is returned to Sue in the same format used by Pearl; the use
	of Speedy instead of Pearl is transparent to Sue except for the 
	value of DPC_TIMING(simulator).

    After dpc is complete, the user can invoke Speedy commands to modify
	the DESIGN data base (for example, "speedy resize") and display the
	timing based on those changes without reflecting them into Sue.

	* sue> speedy global_timing
		compute and display the current long path.  

	* sue> speedy print long_delay
		compute and give the value of the current long delay,
		without displaying the path


    Timing sources and destinations

	Timing sources are considered to be:
		* clock input to flipflops  
		* extconns connected to nets with no explicit sources
		* globals
		* nets marked as constant in constraints
		* nets with no sources

	Timing destinations are considered to be:
		* extconns connected to nets that do have explicit sources
		* inports of flipflops, except clock

		cells are designated as flipflops either in their 
		    definition in a .lib file, or manually in a ".fixfile"

    Setup and Hold constraints:
	* timing destinations may have one setup constraints, which 
	    should be to a clock net
	* clock nets are assumed to have "nominal_slope"
	* non-timing-destinations may not have a setup constraint
	* hold constraints are not permited (Speedy doesn't do short paths)
	
	(unpermitted constraints in a .lib file will be ignored)

 	
    RC net delay

	Speedy will include net metal in capacitive load if steiner
	  routing has been done.

	As noted, rc net delays are not successfuly implemented.

	To run Pearl without rc net delays, from the Sue "sim"
	  pull-down menu, select "select parasitic extraction"
	  and un-check the box "DSPF (RC)"

xxx this is very unfortunately broken.
xxx	if "use_rc_net_delay" is true,
xxx		for each segment of the Steiner route, a resistance 
xxx		  and a capacitance number is calculated based on 
xxx		  variables "cconstx", "cconsty", "rconstx", and 
xxx		  "rconsty", which must be set according to the 
xxx		  technology.
xxx		an RC time constant is calculated for each node in the
xxx		  net, based on the total resistance to the source and
xxx		  the total capacitance in the remaining directions 
xxx		for each INPORT, the time constants along the path 
xxx		  from the connected NET source to the INPORT are 
xxx		  summed, and the result is stored in the INPORT as 
xxx		  "net_delay" 
xxx		the INPORT's net_delay is added to paths traversing
xxx		  the input.
xxx		
xxx		... this algorithm doesn't take account of variable
xxx		  net width, effect of via's, or different constants 
xxx		  for differnt metal layers.
xxx
xxx		... we should figure the slope degradation, but I
xxx		  don't know how to do that.  INPORT slope is assumed
xxx		  to be the same as the NET source's slope.  
xxx

    "cap_fudge"
	The idea (says Lee) is that since DPC is approximating the location
	  of pins on cells as the center of the cell, add a small amount of
	  capacitance to a net to ensure that short nets have some.  Sue makes
	  up the number and passes it with net information in the call to 
	  speedy_begin_net.
	Speedy adds the fudge to the first segment in the steinerized net,
	  from which it gets reflected into outport load capacitance.  Speedy
	  also writes the cap_fudge as a comment in the est_dspf file.  (For
	  an est_cap file, the fudge is already reflected in the net capactance.)
	For whatever reason (ask Lee... he will mumble something about not knowing
	  the location of external pins... since we don't have a ports file.),
	  external nets are not included in the DSPF process, but Speedy forces
	  the external nets to be updated with the cap_fudge for internal use.
	  (Theoretically the fudgy number could be variable with net, but in 
	  practice it is just selected by technology.)

    Constraint file
	(see FILE FORMATS)
	set assumed delay at external connections
	set assumed external load capacitance 
	fix nets as "constant"


    Long path algorithm

	Speedy constructs an ordering of all INSTANCEs which is essentially
	"left to right" (GLOBAL_DOWNSTREAM)

	Speedy walks down the list of instances; for each instance,
	the delay to the inputs is known.  "He" calculates all the arcs 
	defined in the ".lib" file; for each instance OUTPORT, the delay to 
	the OUTPORT is taken as the maximum of (delay to inport) + (delay of
	arc from inport to outport).  Rising and falling edges (at the 
	outport) are computed and stored separately.

	Finally, Speedy walks over the timing destinations looking for the
	maximum delay.
	

    "saved path"
	The current long path can be saved for later re-evaluation under
	different conditions, or a path can be constructed.

		* sue> speedy save_long_path
			store the present long path as the saved path

		* sue> speedy create_saved_path <net name> {'^' | 'v'}
		* sue> speedy add_to_saved_path <net name> {'^' | 'v'}
		* sue> speedy complete_saved_path <instance or external connection name>

		* sue> speedy time_saved_path
			compute along the saved path and display; the delay times
			shown are along the path
		* sue> speedy print saved_path
			*without* recalculating, display the path elements; so the 
			delay times shown are due to whatever recent global_timing
			and represent the longest delay to that point... may or may
			not be derived from the preceeding element in the saved path




CELL RESIZING
-------------------

    Nomenclature:
	INSTANCE:	one physical group of transistors; it has a 
			unique pathname, and a type which refers to a 
			basic cell type.

	CELL:		a generic type, described in some ".lib" file;
			it has a specific drive strength, &c.
	
	CLONE:		the set of instances that derive from a single
			icon in sue; if the intent is to store the data
			back into sue, all clones must have the same
			cell type.

	FUNCTIONGROUP:	A set of functionally equivalent cells with
			various drive strengths, A through E.

    INSTANCEs can be individually resized in Speedy, it is 
	updated in the DESIGN data base so that in the future, timing
	commands will see the new cell.  The instance keeps its 
	original name.

	It is more usual to resize all the instances in a CLONE at
	once, so that the data can be written back to sue; however, it
	is possible to resize INSTANCEs as individuals.

	INSTANCEs can be marked as not resizeable in the .fixfile
	(see FILE FORMATS, .fixfile)

	 * dont_resize path <hierarchical name>
	 * dont_resize module <type name> 

    RE-PLACEMENT: Note that resizing a gate upwards may disturb the 
	placement.  In order to be entirely believable, a resize result 
	must be fed back into SUE and a new DPC placement made.
	The resize algorithms write a file for the purpose, which can
	be invoked on the sue command line:

	* sue> source make_resizes.tcl

	(there used to be a "display_resizes" option.... is there
	interest in restoring it?)

RESIZE METHODS:

	* sue> speedy resize <method name>

    <method name>:
        <default>               ... I-IV by clones
        instances               ... I-II by instances, III-IV by clones
        thresholds              ... I by clones
        downsize                ... II by clones
        optimize_path           ... III by clones
        for_area                ... IV by clones
        thresholds_by_instance  ... I by instances
        downsize_by_instance    ... II by instances
        for_area_by_instances   ... IV by instances
        minimum
        maximum

    STEP I: "thresholds"  
	Select the size (drive) of all INSTANCEs so that
	all output slopes are as close as may be to a target 
	slope.  

	* speedy {set | print} slope <value in nanoseconds>
		set the nominal-slope

    STEP II: "downsize"
	Each instance (or clone) is examined to determine whether 
	reducing the drive of the instance will speed up the local
	path... that is, a typical 3-gate path around the target 
	instance.  This is not a complete retiming, just a local 
	guess.  

	The original idea was to correct for irregularities in the 
	cell library, for example MMI_NAND4 in mmi25, where the 
	'C' size circuit has extra buffering, and therefore more
	intrinsic delay as well as more drive.

    STEP III: "optimize_path"
	The algorithm tries to reduce the size of side branches 
	in order to reduce the load on the critical path.
	(If the long path changes in the course of this, the
	algorithm will continue by optimizing the new long path.)

    STEP IV: "downsize_for_area"
	For each instance off the critical path, the algorithm
	will downsize the instance if it can do so without 
	increasing the maximum path delay.  



    Each of the above can be done by-clones (in which case the 
	resize is only accepted if it works for all instances in 
	the clone) or by-instances.

    DEFAULT is Step I-IV by_clones.

    also available:
	maximum/minimum: set all resizeable instances to be 
	  as large/small as possible
	optimize_path: see "create_saved_path"; optimize the
	  named path, rather than the design long path

DATA BASE STRUCTURE
------------------------

	These are the major classes which are used to build up the
	design database; there are naturally additional classes
	associated with the particular functional areas, as described 
	elsewhere.

	(Class names are all capital letters, as INSTANCE)

	(Note that all these things are fully expanded; that is, none
	of these things are represented as arrays.  So that from
	speedy's point of view a net called "net[1]" has no particular
	relation to a net called "net[2]").

	DESIGN -- the present schematic, in the Flat World 
	Primary types:
		NET		.. has a single origin (an OUTPORT)
				.. may be marked as various kinds of
				   constant or as a clock net

		INSTANCE	.. a particular gate
				.. points to a CELL

		EXTCONN		.. an external connection (note that
				   since a net has only one source, 
				   signals always cross an extconn in 
				   only one direction)

	    .. a port is a connection between a NET and an INSTANCE 
	       (common to both, points to both)
	    .. has a particular location

		INPORT		.. a signal sink; an input to a
				   particular gate or an external
				   connnection output 
				.. points to an INPIN
				.. has a net_delay from net source

		OUTPORT		.. a signal source; an output of a
				   particular gate or an external
				   connection input 
				.. points to an OUTPIN
				.. has a load capacitance (net
				   capacitance + connected inports)
	
		
		NODE		.. a defined intermediate point on a
				   wire (a junction); not connected to
				   a gate or external connection 
				.. a kind of port... has a particular
				   location 


		SEGMENT		.. a chunk of a wire, from one
				   INPORT/OUTPORT/NODE to another
				.. has a resistance and a capacitance


	CELL_LIBRARY

		CELL		.. a generic gate, eg MMI_NAND2A
				.. has a list of INPINs and OUTPINs
				.. has size, &tc.

	    Corresponding to INPORT & OUTPORT; contains timing tables,
	    load capacitance, etc.

		INPIN	

		OUTPIN 


	HIERARCHY
	
	    We retain the heirachical view implied in the Verilog
	    netlist.  An instance of class HIERARCHY corresponds to 
	    a Verilog "module".

		CLONE	.. the set of INSTANCEs derived from a
			single icon in some SUE cell (that is, a 
			particular instance in some Verilog module)
	

	list classes

	    Groups of things are implemented as Lisp-like
		singly-linked lists, using separate list elements,
		defined by "ListOfWHATNOT" classes. (Template classes 
		are not used, for many good reasons.)  


	not supported:
	    - multi-phase clocks
	    - negative-edge flipflops
	    - multi-source nets - tristate 
		



STANDALONE MODE
---------------

	In standalone mode, loading is driven by the "speedy.cmd" file
	  which must be supplied by the user (or manual command line 
	  entries.  A typical command file would contain the following

		* read the cell libraries	  
	read_cell_library /proj/tech/mmi25/library/synopsys/mmi25.lib
	read_cell_library /proj/work/marshall/malleable/rams/DCV.lib

		* set some additional process constants
	set rconstx .1833333
	set rconsty .1833333
	set cconstx .00022
	set cconsty .00022

		* read the gate-level verilog, construct the design
	set top_level_cellname	mdp1
	read_vgfile mdp1.vg
	
		* read back the dspf file for location information
		  ... recalculate the steiner route
	read_dspffile mdp1.est_dspf

		* read additional user-supplied information
	read_fixfile mdp1.fixfile
	read_timing_in_file mdp1.constraint

		* now do work.... for instance
	global_timing
	print cell_area
	set slope .120
	resize
	global_timing
	print cell_area


GLOBAL ROUTING
--------------------

    The global routing algorithm

	Speedy will divide the bounding box of the top-level SUE cell
	  into GRIDBOXes of specified size; the obvious size is a 
	  row size by one bit pitch; eg 10 x 22 for the Malleable
	  chip.  The number of horizontal and vertical channels
	  available can be set for each GRIDBOX individually; the
	  default assumption is one channel per grid unit.

	He then routes the SEGMENTs of the DESIGN... each segment is
	  just described by two PORTs, which are the corners of a 
	  bounding box... as long as the SEGMENT stays inside the 
	  box, and proceeds Manhattan-wise monotonicly towards the 
	  opposite corner, the SEGMENT will have the minimum length
	  implied by the steiner route.

	Line SEGMENTs are routed first (the two ports are in the same
	  column or the same row of GRIDBOXes).  The SEGMENT is given
	  a list of GRIDBOXes, and the SEGMENT is added to a list of 
	  SEGMENTS in each GRIDBOX traversed.

	Then he routes open SEGMENTs, where he has to actually make
	  choices.  Somewhat similar to the "global_timing"
	  algorithm, he starts from one PORT and propagates the 
	  route forwards in all possible ways (within the bounding
	  box), keeping track of the cheapest route to each GRIBOX.
	  Finally, he starts at the opposite PORT and follows the 
	  cheapest route backwards.  This route is recorded in the
	  SEGMENT and in the GRIDBOXes as above.

	"Cheap" means that GRIDBOXes traversed are relatively empty.
	  For a nearly-empty GRIDBOX, the congestion number is the 
	  number of wires.  When the number of wires rises above a
	  configurable "low-water" number, the number of wires is
	  multiplied by a configurable factor (right now, 100). 
	  When the number of wires exceeds the physical number of 
	  channels (actually the configurable "high-water" limit,
	  the number of wires is multiplied by a rather larger factor
	  (right now, 10000).

	Actually separate numbers are maintained for horizontal and
	  vertical congestion, and what is actually being counted is
	  the number of wires traversing the right and lower edges
	  of the GRIDBOX (internal wires generate a count on both 
	  edges).
	  
    Display

	An overview of the congestion results can be displayed on the
	  SUE dpc layout screen.  Nothing is shown for "nearly-empty"
	  GRIDBOXes.  If a GRIDBOX has a vertical or horizontal
	  congestion above lowwater, a solid box will be shown at
	  the GRIDBOX location where the size of the size is
	  proportional to the degree of congestion; if the GRIDBOX
	  is just at the highwater mark, the box will be half the
	  dimensions of the GRIDBOX.  If either horizontal or vertical
	  congestion is above highwater, the box is red; otherwise
	  the box is yellow.
	
	Speedy will also produce a summary or a list of of GRIDBOXes
	  that are nearly empty, crowded, or overfull.
	
	The routing of a NET selected by name can be displayed; a
	  green line is shown running through whichever GRIDBOXes.
	  PORTs on the NET are marked with small crosses.  (These 
	  crosses are in the correct gridbox, but they are not at 
	  the exact PORT location.)  Also, the NET's SEGMENTs are
	  listed (printf'd to the console window), with a list of
	  GRIDBOXes for each. 

	An individual GRIDBOX can be selected by selecting any cell
	  whose origin is inside the GRIDBOX, or by specifying it by
	  coordinates on the command line.  All the nets that are 
	  routed through the selected GRIDBOX are displayed as above;
	  NETs are diagonally offset so as not to overlap on the
	  display.  Also, the NETs are listed on the console.

	All the nets connected to a named INSTANCE can be displayed.


    Improving the Global Route

	I made some attempt to shove NETs around to improve the
	  overall congestion:
		* find a highly-congested gridbox
		* pick a segment passing through it
		* unroute and reroute it
		* repeat until tired
	  With not very good results.  If there are a few isolated
	  very bad GRIDBOXes, we can make some improvement, but very
	  rapidly you "beat the lumps down over here, but they pop up
	  over there".

	The thing to do would be to allow SEGMENTs to get longer in 
	  order to go around congested areas.  I wrote an algorithm 
	  to do this... it's similar to the steiner routing algorithm,
	  but rather slower.  To be useful, it needs some more 
	  intelligence in selecting SEGMENTs that can be rerouted
	  and in selecting a bounding box for the new route.

	This sounds like the dreaded "timing-driven route" which must
	  mean something different than I think it means, because it
	  doesn't look very hard from here.  That is: looking at a 
	  congested area, find a segment passing through that belongs
	  to a net well away from a critical path; figure out how much
	  time it would be safe to add to the segment; translate that
	  to the physical net length it would be safe to add; relate
	  that to a new bounding box; re-(global)-route the segment
	  within the new box to minimize congestion; check that timing
	  constraints have been maintained.  ???

    Presevering the Global Route

	I can easily imagine that by the above sort of refinements
	  (including adjustments to the DPC or floorplan if necessary)
	  we could create a "clean" global route that maintained
	  timing constraints.  If only there were some way to feed 
	  that forward into a detail router....



	
COMMANDS
--------

    I think the right way to think of Speedy is not as a set of
      commands, but as a database that can be used to implement an
      expandable set of functionality, covering whatever can be
      thought of in the "flat world".  Therefore, the current command
      set is the opposite of "cast in concrete"... please talk with
      me about what you wish it would do.

    The intent is to make the commands "do one thing well"...
      probably to support useful work, people will want to cluster
      sets of commands under a single menu tab.... this can be done
      most flexibly by using tcl procs (in SUE mode).  I will be happy
      to work on such procs; people can also do it themselves, it's
      a simple process.  


    Here is a snapshot of the current command set:

	read_command_file <filename>	... take commands from named file
	source <filename>		... take commands from named file
	set <variable> <value>
	    variables: 
		top_level_cellname	... also creates new DESIGN

		rconstx			... physical parms for nets 
		rconsty 
		cconstx 
		cconsty 
		
		nominal_slope		... for clock edges & default
					    (also sets target_slope and
					    computes resize-by-load 
					    thresholds)
		target_slope		... for "compute_thresholds"
		assumed_outport_load
		use_rc_net_delay	... for "global_timing", &c
		upsize_threshold	... for "resize upsize"
		downsize_threshold	... for "resize downsize"
		default_speedy_path	... otherwise set to "/mmi-cad/src/speedy"
		speedy_path		... where to look for .cmd files
		
	print <variable>
	echo <string>			... printf the string

	compute_thresholds		
	write_threshold_file
	print_thresholds
	read_thresholdfile
	characterize <load> <slope>

	quit
	exit

	read_cell_library <filename>
	read_vgfile <filename>	... cell libraries must be loaded
				  previously
				... error messages for:
				  nets with multiple sources
				  instances with unidentifyable cell
				  unidentifyable port names
				  mismatch in assigns

	read_dspffile <filename>  ... design must be loaded previously
				  (read_vgfile)  
				... error messages for:
				  unidentifyable instance/port/net


	read_fixfile <filename>

	check_design		... looks for problems in the DESIGN
				prints messages. This is done automaticly
				after "read_vgfile" command (or from
				vgfile is loaded from timing_in file).
				    ... nets with no connections
				    ... nets with no source, except
				     nets with one load called "uc_..." 

				(lots of errors will be caught during 
				read_vgfile itself)

				NOTE: this is an expandable list! What else
				should I be checking for???

	resize <method>		... see above
	clear_resizes
	find_resizes
	print_resizes
	annotate_resizes
	replace_resizes

	save_cell_pointers
	compare_cell_pointers
	restore_cell_pointers
	restore_nominal_cells	... restore all instance cells to what
				  it says in the instance->heirarchy
				  (that is, what Sue thinks the
				  instance->cell should be)

	get_total_cell_area

	print_slow_nets

	clear

	global_timing		... compute the long path to each instance:outport
				  construct design->long_pathlist
	read_timing_in_file <filename>

	compute_net_characteristics

	print_timing_info
	print_long_path

	trace_not_propagated <netname>	... if "global_timing" prints some messages
				"delay not propagated to ..." (and usually if he prints
				one, he prints a bunch...), this debug function will
				swim upstream looking for the source of the problem

	save_long_path		... copy of current long path to saved_path

	create_saved_path <netname>  ... allows user to create (and then time) an
					arbitrary path by supplying a list of
					net names; eg, 
						create_saved_path <origin netname>
						add_to_saved_path <next netname>
							....
						add_to_saved_path <destination netname>
						end_saved_path
						time_saved_path
					if a net doesn't connect through one instance
					to the previous net, an error message is printed
	add_to_saved_path <netname>
	complete_saved_path <instance or external pin name>

	time_saved_path
	print_saved_path
	optimize_saved_path
